Welcome to the interactive exhibition of strategic and critical minerals

Take the exhibition with youScan with your phone

Explore the different sections of the exhibition to discover the raw materials essential to the economy, whose availability in the European Union is at risk due to high import dependence and the concentration of supply in a few countries.

Fundamental / critical raw materials

Of great economic importance for all of European industry, with a high risk of supply disruption

Some critical raw materials are, in addition, strategic: the European Union considers them essential for green and digital transition technologies, defense and the aerospace sector. Their demand will grow strongly in the coming years and increasing their production is difficult, so securing their supply is a priority.

Strategic raw materials

Essential for key technologies in the green, digital, aerospace and defense transition, with exponential growth in demand forecast

Other strategic elements and minerals

Not included in the current European Union list, but essential for the energy transition and modern industry

Key targets for 2030

The European Union wants to secure the supply of strategic raw materials and reduce its dependence on external suppliers through several targets to be met by 2030.

These targets aim to boost extraction and processing within the European Union, increase recycling and diversify supplier countries to avoid excessive dependence on a single territory.

Extraction

The European Union intends to obtain through domestic extraction at least 10% of its annual consumption of strategic raw materials. This target seeks to make better use of the mineral resources available in European territory, promote new sustainable mining activities and reduce dependence on imports.

Processing

The target is set that at least 40% of annual consumption of strategic raw materials can be met through processing activities carried out within the European Union. Developing its own capacities would generate greater added value, strengthen European industry and reduce vulnerability to disruptions in international supply.

Recycling

The European Union aims to obtain through recycling at least 25% of annual consumption of strategic raw materials. Reaching this goal will require improving the collection and recovery of materials contained in used products, industrial waste, electronic devices, batteries and other technologies.

Supply diversification

The European Union seeks to avoid excessive dependence on a single supplier country. For this reason, it proposes that no more than 65% of annual supply of a strategic raw material comes from a single third country. Diversification aims to reduce the risks associated with conflicts, trade restrictions, logistics crises or political decisions.

Taken together, these objectives seek to strengthen the strategic autonomy, supply security and sustainability of the European Union.

Deposit types and extraction

Antimony (Sb)

Extraction

Antimony comes mainly from stibnite, which forms in hydrothermal veins, almost always with quartz and sometimes with gold. It is extracted in underground and open-pit mines, and the ore is crushed and concentrated by flotation. The concentrate is roasted to obtain antimony oxide or smelted with iron to reduce it to metal.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · Russia · Tajikistan · Bolivia · Turkey · Australia · Vietnam

China accounts for a very significant share of world production.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: technical components, ammunition and fire-resistant materials, used in lightweight armor and protective equipment for military and emergency personnel.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: hardening of lead alloys for lead-acid batteries.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: added as a fining agent to the glass of photovoltaic solar panels, to remove bubbles and improve transparency.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: manufacture of semiconductors such as InSb and GaSb.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: improves the hardness and strength of other metals, forming anti-friction alloys used in industrial bearings.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: antimony trioxide is the most widely used catalyst in the manufacture of PET plastic for bottles and fibers.
  • Civil security and risk protection: use of antimony trioxide (Sb₂O₃) as a flame retardant in plastics, textiles and electrical wiring, reducing the risk of fire.
  • Glass and ceramics: opacifiers, pigments and finishing agents, used in ceramic glazes and in the manufacture of special high-opacity glasses.

Beryllium (Be)

Extraction

Beryllium is obtained from two minerals: beryl, which crystallizes in granitic pegmatites, and bertrandite, deposited by hydrothermal fluids in volcanic tuffs, as at Spor Mountain (USA), the world's main mine. The ore is crushed and concentrated, then chemically treated to obtain beryllium hydroxide, which is converted into metal, copper alloys or beryllium oxide.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

United States · China · Brazil · Madagascar · Mozambique · Portugal

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: used in precision systems, lightweight structures and military equipment components that require strength, dimensional stability and low weight.
  • Aerospace: beryllium is used in components of aircraft, satellites and space systems for its lightness, stiffness and stability under temperature changes.
  • Telecommunications: its alloys, especially copper-beryllium, are used in connectors, electrical contacts, switches and components that require conductivity, elasticity and wear resistance.
  • Nuclear energy: beryllium is used in certain components and systems of nuclear reactors due to its properties as a neutron reflector and moderator.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: it lets X-rays pass through, so it is used for the windows of X-ray tubes and mammography equipment.

Arsenic (As)

Extraction

Arsenic is not usually mined for its own sake: it is recovered as a by-product of copper, gold, lead and cobalt metallurgy, whose ores contain it in minerals such as arsenopyrite or enargite. When these concentrates are roasted or smelted, the arsenic volatilizes and is collected in the furnace dust as arsenic trioxide, which is purified or reduced to metal.

Main minerals

Arsenopyrite, realgar and orpiment.

Main producing countries

Peru, China and Morocco account for most of the world's arsenic production, mainly as arsenic trioxide. There are also smaller productions in countries such as Russia, Belgium and Japan.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: small amounts harden the lead grids of lead-acid batteries.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: use of arsenide-based semiconductors in high-performance solar cells, especially in space applications and specialized photovoltaic systems.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: basis of semiconductors such as gallium arsenide (GaAs) and indium arsenide (InAs), used in lasers, LEDs and infrared sensors.
  • Telecommunications: use of gallium arsenide in high-frequency components, amplifiers, communication systems and wireless devices.

Aluminum (Al)

Extraction

Bauxite forms through intense weathering of aluminum-rich rocks in tropical climates, and is worked in shallow open-pit mines. After crushing, it is converted into alumina by the Bayer process, which dissolves it in hot caustic soda and separates the impurities (the “red mud”). The alumina is then reduced by electrolysis (Hall-Héroult process) to obtain aluminum metal.

Main minerals

Allophane has a variable, non-stoichiometric composition.

Main producing countries

Australia, Guinea, China, Brazil and India.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: use in military vehicles, structures, lightweight equipment and special alloys.
  • Aerospace: use in aircraft and satellites to reduce weight and improve energy efficiency.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: manufacture of lighter cars, electric vehicles, trains and ships, thanks to its low density, corrosion resistance and ease of forming.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: casings for computers and phones, heat sinks and technological components.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: cables for high-voltage power lines, lighter than copper ones, and solar panel frames.
  • Construction and infrastructure: profiles, façades, window frames and lightweight structures in building and infrastructure, thanks to its low weight and corrosion resistance.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: production of cans, trays, aluminum foil and other packaging that protects products from light, oxygen and moisture.

Baryte (BaSO₄)

Extraction

Baryte forms mainly in hydrothermal veins and in sedimentary layers of marine origin, where it occurs as masses or pockets. It is mined in open pits or underground, and the ore is crushed, ground and concentrated by gravity separation, taking advantage of its high density, or by flotation. Most of it is used ground, without further processing, in drilling muds for oil and gas wells.

Main minerals

Baryte, barium sulfate (BaSO₄).

Main producing countries

China, India, Morocco, Mexico and United States.

Strategic applications

  • Medicine and pharmacy: radiation shielding in concrete and linings of medical facilities, and radiological contrast (barium sulfate) for the digestive tract.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: it is essential in drilling muds for oil and gas wells, due to its high density, and is used as a filler in plastics and composite materials.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: baryte is used as a mineral filler in paints, plastics, varnishes and coatings. It provides density, chemical stability, opacity and a uniform finish.
  • Glass and ceramics: used as a raw material to obtain barium compounds and in the manufacture of glass, ceramics and other special materials.

Bismuth (Bi)

Extraction

Bismuth hardly forms deposits of its own: it accompanies, in small amounts, the lead, tungsten, copper and tin minerals of hydrothermal veins. It is recovered as a by-product of refining these metals, especially lead, and then purified by thermal and electrolytic processes.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, Vietnam, Laos, Mexico and Bolivia.

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: It is added to low-melting-point alloys and special solders, especially in electrical and electronic components.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: bismuth subsalicylate and subcitrate are used for upset stomach and for infection by Helicobacter pylori; bismuth oxychloride gives cosmetics a pearly sheen.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: It is added to free-machining steels, aluminum alloys and brasses as a non-toxic substitute for lead.
  • Civil security and risk protection: Its low-melting alloys are used in thermal fuses and fire sprinklers, and, being non-toxic, it replaces lead in ammunition and components.
  • Glass and ceramics: Its compounds are used in the manufacture of optical glass, pigments and materials with specific properties.

Boron (B)

Extraction

Boron comes from borates such as borax, colemanite or ulexite, which precipitate when salt lakes evaporate in volcanic and arid areas; the largest deposits are in Turkey, the USA and the Andes. They are mined in open pits or obtained from brines, and the ore is dissolved, purified and recrystallized to produce borax, boric acid and other boron compounds.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Turkey, United States, Argentina, Chile and Peru.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: boron carbide (B₄C), an extremely hard and lightweight ceramic, is used in personal and vehicle armor plates.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: component of the neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnets used in electric motors and wind turbines, and also used in glass for photovoltaic panels.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: manufacture of semiconductors, dopants for silicon and materials used in advanced electronic devices.
  • Nuclear energy: use of boron carbide and other compounds in armor, wear-resistant materials and neutron-absorption systems in nuclear facilities.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: small amounts of boron increase the hardenability of high-strength steels used in cars, machinery and structures under stress.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: essential micronutrient for plant growth, vital for cell wall formation and flowering; borax and boric acid are used as fertilizers.
  • Glass and ceramics: manufacture of borosilicate glass, fiberglass, enamels and heat-resistant ceramics, used in construction, industry and solar panels.

Coking coal

Extraction

Coal forms from plant remains accumulated in swamps and peat bogs, buried and transformed over millions of years by pressure and heat. Only some bituminous coals, the coking coals, are suitable for making coke. They are extracted in underground and open-pit mines, washed to remove ash and sulfur, and heated without air to about 1,000-1,100 °C in coke oven batteries.

Main minerals

Not a mineral: an organic sedimentary rock (C)

Coal is a rock formed from transformed plant remains, not a mineral. Coking coal is a medium-rank bituminous coal that, when heated, softens and agglomerates to form a strong, porous coke.

Main producing countries

China, Australia, Russia, United States, Canada and Mongolia.

China is the largest producer and consumer of coking coal, and Australia its largest exporter.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: the steel for armor, ships and military vehicles is mostly made in blast furnaces that depend on coke.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: coal tar pitch, a by-product of coking, is a raw material for needle coke and the synthetic graphite in battery anodes.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: this is its main use: in the blast furnace, coke supplies heat, reduces the iron ore and keeps the charge permeable to gases; it is also used in foundries and ferroalloys.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: coking produces tar, benzene, naphthalene and ammonia, as well as the pitch used to make electrodes and anodes for steel and aluminum.

It is also considered a strategic material because of its high economic importance, a supply that cannot be increased quickly and Europe's heavy dependence on imports. It will still be needed during the transition to lower-emission steelmaking.

Cobalt (Co)

Extraction

Cobalt is almost never mined on its own: it is obtained as a by-product of copper, especially in the Copperbelt of the DR Congo, and of nickel, from both sulfides and laterites. The ore is concentrated and processed hydrometallurgically (leaching, solvent extraction and electrolysis) to obtain cobalt metal or cobalt sulfate for batteries.

Main minerals

Cobaltite, heterogenite and asbolane; also nickel-cobalt lateritic minerals.

Main producing countries

DR Congo, Indonesia, Russia, Australia and Philippines.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: forms samarium-cobalt and Alnico permanent magnets, which retain their strength at high temperatures and are used in military, aerospace and guidance systems.
  • Aerospace: manufacture of aircraft turbines, engines and equipment exposed to high temperatures. It improves resistance to heat, corrosion and fatigue, increasing the durability of materials.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: component of the cathodes of many lithium-ion batteries, providing energy density and stability during charge cycles.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy and in the sterilization of medical supplies and food.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: cemented carbides and cutting tools, giving them hardness and resistance to high temperatures.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: catalyst in petroleum refining (hydrodesulfurization) and in the synthesis of fuels and chemicals.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: production of blue pigments and driers for paints and varnishes, providing color, opacity and stability.

Copper (Cu)

Extraction

Most copper comes from porphyry copper deposits, huge masses of rock with disseminated sulfides that are worked in large open pits. The sulfides are crushed, concentrated by flotation, smelted and refined by electrolysis. Oxidized ores, on the other hand, are dissolved with acid (leaching), and the copper is recovered by solvent extraction and electrowinning. Recycling also makes an important contribution.

Main minerals

The most important copper minerals include sulfides, such as chalcopyrite, bornite, chalcocite and covellite, and oxidized minerals, such as cuprite, azurite, malachite, chrysocolla, dioptase, shattuckite and conichalcite.

Main producing countries

Chile, Peru, DR Congo, China and United States.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: electric vehicles, charging stations and storage systems, where it enables electrical conduction and the connection of energy infrastructure components.
  • Defense and security: brass (an alloy of copper and zinc) is the standard material for ammunition cartridge cases, and is also used in electrical components of defense systems.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: printed circuits, connectors, computer equipment and communication systems, for its ability to transmit signals and current efficiently.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: cables, transformers, motors, generators and distribution systems, thanks to its high electrical conductivity and ease of forming.
  • Construction and infrastructure: water and gas pipes, building wiring, heat exchangers, roofing and brass and bronze fittings.

Scandium

Extraction

Scandium has no mines of its own: it is scattered through many rocks and is obtained only as a by-product, mainly when nickel laterites and residues from titanium dioxide pigment production are treated with acid. It is separated by solvent extraction, precipitated and calcined to obtain scandium oxide, which is used in aluminum alloys and fuel cells.

Main minerals

There are scandium minerals of its own, such as thortveitite, but they are very rare and are not mined as ores. Scandium is obtained as a by-product of processing other ores: residues from titanium pigment production, bauxite red mud, nickel laterites and rare-earth or uranium ores.

No ore of its own: obtained as a by-product.

Main producing countries

China, Philippines, Russia, Kazakhstan and Canada.

It is a very small market, of tens of tonnes per year, in which China is the leading producer.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: aluminum-scandium alloys are lighter and stronger, making it possible to build weldable, high-performance structures for aircraft and aerospace systems.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: scandium oxide stabilizes the zirconia in the electrolytes of solid oxide fuel cells, improving their performance and durability.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: scandium iodide is used in very bright metal halide lamps, and scandium is also found in some laser crystals.
  • Telecommunications: aluminum scandium nitride is used in radio-frequency filters for wireless communications such as 5G.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: used in lightweight alloys for 3D printing and in high-performance sports equipment, such as bicycle frames.

Strontium (Sr)

Extraction

Strontium comes from celestine (strontium sulfate), which forms in evaporite layers alongside gypsum; the province of Granada hosts one of the main deposits in the world. It is mined open-pit and concentrated by gravity separation and flotation. It is then chemically converted into strontium carbonate, the raw material from which the other compounds are made.

Main minerals

Celestine (SrSO₄) is the main commercial ore of strontium. Strontianite (SrCO₃) is less abundant, but is also a natural source of this element.

Main producing countries

Iran, Spain (Granada), China and Mexico.

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: strontium ferrite is used in permanent magnets for electric motors, loudspeakers, generators and electronic equipment.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: the radioisotope strontium-89 is used in the palliative treatment of pain caused by bone metastases.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: added to aluminum-silicon alloys to refine their structure and improve their mechanical properties.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: ground celestine, in drilling muds for oil and gas wells, is its main use.
  • Civil security and risk protection: its salts give the red color of fireworks and flares, and strontium aluminate forms phosphorescent signaling pigments.
  • Glass and ceramics: its compounds are involved in the manufacture of special glasses, ceramics, glazes and optical materials.

Feldspar

Extraction

Feldspars are the most abundant group of minerals in the Earth's crust. They are mined in pegmatites and altered granites, and also in feldspathic sands, almost always in open-pit quarries. The ore is crushed, ground and separated from quartz and mica by flotation and magnetic separation, to obtain high-purity raw materials for glass and ceramics.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

The main producing countries are Turkey, India, Iran, China, Italy, Thailand and Spain.

Strategic applications

  • Metallurgical and steel industry: used in mild abrasives, welding electrodes and certain composite-material applications, taking advantage of its hardness and chemical stability.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: in powdered form, it acts as a mineral filler and extender, providing stability, wear resistance and durability to various industrial products.
  • Glass and ceramics: essential flux for glass and ceramics (tiles, sanitaryware, tableware, porcelain and glazes), because it supplies alumina and alkalis and promotes vitrification.

Fluorite (CaF₂)

Extraction

Fluorite is deposited from hydrothermal fluids, in veins and in bodies that replace limestones. It is mined underground and in open pits, and concentrated by crushing, grinding and flotation. Depending on its purity it is classified as acid grade (more than 97% calcium fluoride), used to make hydrofluoric acid, or as metallurgical and ceramic grades.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, Mexico, Mongolia, South Africa and Spain.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: fluorinated derivatives are part of the electrolytes and binders of lithium-ion batteries.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: its fluorinated derivatives are used in the manufacture and protection of photovoltaic panels.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: its crystals, transparent to ultraviolet and infrared, are used in precision lenses, and its derivatives in semiconductor manufacturing.
  • Nuclear energy: uranium hexafluoride, obtained with fluorine from fluorite, is the compound used to enrich uranium for nuclear power plants.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: acts as a flux in steelmaking, and its derivatives are used in aluminum production.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: it is the main source of fluorine for hydrofluoric acid, the basis of refrigerants, fluoropolymers and other chemicals.
  • Glass and ceramics: used as a flux and opacifier in glass, glazes and ceramics, improving their melting and final properties.

Phosphorite

Extraction

Phosphorite is a sedimentary rock of marine origin, formed on shelves where cold currents bring nutrients and the remains of phosphate-rich organisms accumulate. It is mined in large open-pit mines, and the ore is washed, screened and concentrated by flotation. The concentrate is treated with sulfuric acid to make phosphoric acid and fertilizers.

Main minerals

Apatite and francolite-group minerals.

Main producing countries

China, Morocco, United States, Russia and Jordan.

Morocco and Western Sahara hold more than two thirds of the world's reserves.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: purified phosphoric acid is a raw material for lithium iron phosphate (LFP), used in battery cathodes for electric vehicles and energy storage.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: basis of phosphate fertilizers, with no substitute in agriculture, and of feed phosphates; part is used to make elemental phosphorus.
  • Environmental management and water treatment: phosphoric acid and its derivatives are used in detergents, water treatment, food additives and corrosion protection.

Phosphorus

Extraction

Phosphorus comes from phosphate rock: mainly marine sedimentary phosphorites and, to a lesser extent, apatite from carbonatites and alkaline rocks, as on the Kola Peninsula (Russia). To obtain the element, the rock is mixed with coke and silica and heated in electric furnaces to about 1,400 °C; the phosphorus is released as vapor and condensed under water as white phosphorus. The process uses a lot of electricity.

Main minerals

Apatite and francolite in phosphate rocks.

Main producing countries

China, Kazakhstan, Vietnam and United States.

China holds most of the world's capacity. Europe has not produced elemental phosphorus since 2012 and depends on imports, mainly from Kazakhstan, Vietnam and China.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: high-purity phosphoric acid is a raw material for lithium iron phosphate (LFP), which is used in battery cathodes for electric vehicles and energy storage.
  • Telecommunications: high-purity phosphorus is used in indium phosphide, key to fiber optics and 5G communications, and as a dopant in silicon chip manufacturing.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: is part of phosphor bronzes, resistant to wear and corrosion, used in springs, connectors and bearings.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: it is the basis of herbicides such as glyphosate and of food- and pharmaceutical-grade phosphates, used as additives in the food industry.
  • Environmental management and water treatment: its derivatives are used as agents in the treatment of industrial water and wastewater.
  • Civil security and risk protection: its compounds are added to plastics, textiles and electronic components as flame retardants, and it is used in pyrotechnics and signal ammunition.

Gallium (Ga)

Extraction

Gallium has no deposits of its own: it substitutes in small amounts for aluminum in bauxite and for zinc in sphalerite. It is recovered as a by-product of the Bayer process, from whose liquors it is extracted by ion exchange and electrolysis, and to a lesser extent from zinc refining. The metal is then purified to the extreme purity required by semiconductors.

Main minerals

It is not usually mined from its own minerals; it occurs associated with bauxite and sphalerite.

Main producing countries

China, Russia, Japan and South Korea.

China accounts for virtually all of the world's primary gallium production.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: gallium semiconductors are the basis of advanced radars, electronic warfare systems and military communications.
  • Aerospace: very high-efficiency gallium arsenide multi-junction solar cells for satellites and space probes.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: gallium nitride (GaN) makes it possible to build fast chargers and compact, efficient converters and inverters for electric vehicles, data centers and power grids.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: gallium arsenide is used in high-frequency circuits for mobile phones, radars and satellites, and gallium is part of LEDs, lasers and sensors.

Germanium (Ge)

Extraction

Germanium does not form deposits of its own: it is recovered as a by-product of zinc refining and from the ash of certain lignites, which concentrate it. These materials are chemically treated to obtain germanium tetrachloride and dioxide, which are reduced to metal and purified by zone refining to the purity required by electronics and infrared optics.

Main minerals

There are germanium minerals of its own, such as argyrodite, in which the element was discovered in 1886, but they are very rare and are not mined as ores. Germanium is obtained as a by-product of processing zinc ores, especially sphalerite, and from the ash of some coals.

No ore of its own: obtained as a by-product.

Main producing countries

China, Belgium, Canada, Russia, Germany and United States.

China is the world's leading producer, with more than two thirds of refined germanium.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: as it is transparent to infrared radiation, it is used in lenses and windows for thermal cameras, night vision systems, sensors and surveillance and guidance equipment.
  • Aerospace: germanium substrates form the base of the multi-junction solar cells that power satellites and space probes.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: silicon-germanium (SiGe) alloys are used in high-speed circuits and wireless communications, and high-purity germanium in gamma-ray detectors.
  • Telecommunications: germanium tetrachloride is used as a dopant in the core of silica optical fibers, which transmit data over long distances with very low losses.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: germanium dioxide acts as a catalyst in the manufacture of PET plastics.

Graphite (C)

Extraction

Natural graphite forms when organic matter in sedimentary rocks is transformed by metamorphism, giving flakes in schists and gneisses or massive graphite in veins. It is mined open-pit or underground, then crushed, ground and concentrated by flotation. Graphite for batteries is purified, rounded and coated. Synthetic graphite is also made from petroleum coke.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, Mozambique, Madagascar, Brazil, Canada, India, Ukraine and Norway.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: It is the essential material in lithium-ion battery anodes, key to electrifying transport and storing renewable energy.
  • Nuclear energy: High-purity graphite acts as a neutron moderator in some types of nuclear reactors.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: It is used in crucibles and refractories, and graphite electrodes carry the current in the arc furnaces that melt scrap to make steel.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: Thanks to its layered structure and low friction, it is used as a solid lubricant in machinery and mechanisms subjected to demanding conditions of temperature or pressure.

Hafnium

Extraction

Hafnium is not mined on its own: it accompanies zirconium in zircon, in a ratio of roughly 1 to 50, and zircon comes mainly from coastal sand placers. It is obtained as a by-product when purifying zirconium for the nuclear industry, which must be free of hafnium: the two are separated by solvent extraction and the hafnium is then reduced to metal.

Main minerals

Zircon and other zirconium minerals.

Main producing countries

France, United States, China, Russia and India.

It is produced in only a few countries, where zirconium metal is manufactured, and there are no reliable public data on world production.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: its carbides and ceramics, with some of the highest known melting points, are being developed for nozzles and thermal protection of rockets and hypersonic vehicles.
  • Aerospace: hafnium-bearing superalloys improve the resistance to oxidation and high temperatures of turbine blades in aircraft engines and gas turbines.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: hafnium oxide is used as a gate insulator in the transistors of advanced chips and in some memories.
  • Nuclear energy: absorbs neutrons efficiently, so it is used in control rods for nuclear reactors, including those for naval propulsion.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: used in plasma-cutting torch electrodes and in optical coatings.

Helium

Extraction

Helium forms in the crust through the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium, and accumulates in some natural gas fields, trapped beneath impermeable rock layers. It is recovered as a by-product of gas: it is separated from the other components by cooling them to very low temperatures (cryogenic separation), and then purified and liquefied for transport.

Main minerals

Does not form its own minerals (He)

It does not form exploitable minerals; it is found as gas trapped in geological deposits.

Main producing countries

United States, Qatar, Algeria, Russia and Canada.

The United States and Qatar produce nearly three quarters of the world's helium.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: used to pressurize and purge the cryogenic fuel tanks of rockets and other space systems.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: used as an inert gas and coolant in the manufacture of chips and optical fiber, where very clean atmospheres and precise temperature control are needed.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: it provides a protective atmosphere for welding reactive metals and makes it possible to detect very small leaks in vacuum systems and critical equipment.
  • Advanced instrumentation: it has no substitute for reaching temperatures close to absolute zero: liquid helium cools the magnets of MRI scanners, particle accelerators and quantum computers.

Heavy rare earths

Extraction

Heavy rare earths come mainly from ion-adsorption clays in southern China and Myanmar, formed by the weathering of granites in a tropical climate, in which the elements are held on the surface of the clays. They are released by injecting salt solutions (leaching) and then separated one by one by solvent extraction. Xenotime is a secondary source.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, Myanmar, Australia, Russia and Brazil.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: yttrium is used in thermal coatings for turbines and engines, and other elements in guidance, radar and sonar systems.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: dysprosium and terbium improve the heat resistance of the neodymium magnets used in electric motors and wind turbines.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: europium, terbium and yttrium make up the phosphors (light-emitting substances) in energy-saving lamps, LEDs and screens.
  • Telecommunications: erbium, ytterbium and holmium are used in lasers and in fiber-optic amplifiers.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: gadolinium is used as a contrast agent in magnetic resonance imaging scans.
  • Nuclear energy: gadolinium absorbs neutrons very efficiently and is used to control nuclear reactors.

Light rare earths

Extraction

Light rare earths come from two deposit types: carbonatites with bastnäsite, such as Bayan Obo (China) or Mountain Pass (USA), and coastal sand placers with monazite. The ore is concentrated by flotation or by magnetic and gravity separation, dissolved with acids, and the elements (lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium…) are separated by solvent extraction.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, United States, Australia, Myanmar and Brazil.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: neodymium and praseodymium form the magnets in electric vehicle motors and wind turbines, and lanthanum is used in nickel-metal hydride batteries.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: neodymium magnets are found in speakers, headphones, hard drives and the vibration motor of phones.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: cerium and lanthanum are used in automotive catalytic converters and in the catalytic cracking of petroleum.
  • Glass and ceramics: cerium is used in polishing precision glass, and lanthanum in high-refractive-index optical lenses.

Lithium (Li)

Extraction

Lithium comes from three deposit types: brines from Andean salt flats, which are concentrated by solar evaporation in large ponds; spodumene pegmatites, worked in hard-rock mines, mainly in Australia; and lake clays from volcanic ash, still under development. In all cases, the concentrate is chemically converted into lithium carbonate or hydroxide for batteries.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Australia, Chile, China, Argentina and Brazil.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: aluminum-lithium alloys, lighter and stiffer, are used in the fuselages and tanks of aircraft and rockets.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: essential for the rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in electronic devices, electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: lithium carbonate is a benchmark medication in the treatment of bipolar disorder.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: its compounds are used as fluxes in the continuous casting of steel and in aluminum production.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: butyllithium acts as an initiator in the manufacture of synthetic rubber, and lithium compounds are involved in the synthesis of drugs and polymers.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: used in high-performance greases that keep their properties under demanding temperature and operating conditions.
  • Glass and ceramics: improves thermal shock resistance and reduces thermal expansion, making more stable and durable materials possible.

Magnesium (Mg)

Extraction

Magnesium is obtained from sedimentary carbonate rocks such as dolostone, from magnesite, and from brines and seawater. Most of the metal is produced in China by calcining dolostone and reducing it with ferrosilicon at high temperature (Pidgeon process); the rest by electrolysis of magnesium chloride extracted from brines. Magnesite is used mainly to make refractories.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, Russia, Israel, Kazakhstan and Turkey.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: its lightweight alloys reduce the weight of aircraft, vehicles and military equipment without losing strength.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: used in castings such as housings, brackets and steering components to make vehicles lighter, saving fuel or extending the range of electric vehicles.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: its lightweight alloys are used in the casings of laptops, cameras and mobile phones.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: alloying element for aluminum and desulfurizer for steel, it is the reducing agent used to obtain titanium and zirconium; magnesite yields refractories for furnaces.

Manganese (Mn)

Extraction

Manganese comes mainly from large sedimentary layers of oxides and carbonates formed on the floor of ancient seas, such as those of the Kalahari (South Africa). They are mined open-pit, and the ore is crushed, washed and concentrated. Almost all of it is smelted to make ferromanganese and silicomanganese for the steel industry; a part is dissolved and electrolyzed to obtain high-purity manganese and manganese sulfate for batteries.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

South Africa, Gabon, Australia, China and Ghana.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: high-purity manganese sulfate is used in lithium-ion battery cathodes, and manganese dioxide in alkaline batteries.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: indispensable in steel, to which it is added as ferromanganese and silicomanganese to deoxidize it and give it strength; it also strengthens aluminum alloys.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: it is an essential micronutrient for plants and is supplied in fertilizers and animal feed.

Nickel (battery grade)

Extraction

Nickel comes from two deposit types: sulfides formed in mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks, which are concentrated by flotation and smelted, and laterites, formed by tropical weathering of those same rocks, which are processed in furnaces or dissolved with acid at high pressure. Batteries need high-purity nickel (class 1) or nickel sulfate.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Indonesia, Philippines, Russia, New Caledonia and Australia.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: nickel alloys are used in turbines and engines that withstand high temperatures and heavy mechanical stresses.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: is part of the high-energy-density cathodes of batteries for electric vehicles and storage systems.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: improves resistance to corrosion and heat, and is a key component of stainless steels and superalloys.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: used as a catalyst in the chemical industry and in corrosion-resistant equipment.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: nickel plating protects and decorates metal surfaces against corrosion and wear.

Niobium (Nb)

Extraction

Niobium comes mainly from pyrochlore in carbonatites, igneous rocks made almost entirely of carbonates; the Araxá mine in Brazil produces most of the world's niobium. The ore is concentrated by magnetic separation and flotation, and converted by aluminothermy into ferroniobium for the steel industry, or refined to obtain high-purity oxides and metal.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Brazil, Canada, Nigeria and Rwanda.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: niobium-bearing superalloys are used in aircraft engines, turbines and rockets that operate at high temperatures.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: used in niobium oxide anodes for fast-charging batteries.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: used in capacitors and optical materials, such as high-refractive-index lenses.
  • Construction and infrastructure: small amounts improve mechanical strength and make pipelines, bridges, vehicles and large infrastructure lighter.
  • Advanced instrumentation: niobium alloys with titanium or tin form superconducting magnets for magnetic resonance imaging and particle accelerators.

Platinum-group metals

Extraction

Platinum-group metals are concentrated in layers of mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks, such as those of the Bushveld Complex (South Africa), and in nickel and copper sulfides, such as those of Norilsk (Russia), where they are co-products. The ore is concentrated by flotation, smelted and chemically treated to separate each metal: platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, iridium and osmium. Recycling of catalytic converters is another important source.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

South Africa, Russia, Zimbabwe, Canada and United States.

Strategic applications

  • Energy transition / renewable energy: used in electrolyzers and fuel cells to produce and use hydrogen.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: used in electrical contacts, sensors and data storage components for their stability and conductivity.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: platinum is used in anticancer drugs, such as cisplatin, and in implants and medical devices.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: act as catalysts in the production of nitric acid, the basis of many fertilizers, in petroleum refining and in the manufacture of chemicals.
  • Environmental management and water treatment: platinum, palladium and rhodium form the catalytic converters that reduce polluting exhaust emissions.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: platinum is one of the leading metals in fine jewelry, especially in rings and wedding bands, for its luster, hardness and resistance to tarnishing.

Silicon metal

Extraction

Silicon metal is not mined as such: it is made from high-purity quartz or quartzite, from quartz veins and metamorphic rocks. The rock is reduced with coal, coke or wood chips in electric arc furnaces. The silicon obtained can then be purified, via trichlorosilane, to the grades required by the solar and electronics industries.

Main varieties

Main producing countries

China, Brazil, Norway, France and Australia.

Strategic applications

  • Energy transition / renewable energy: it is the main material of the photovoltaic cells that convert solar radiation into electricity.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: high-purity silicon is the basis of the chips, microprocessors, memories and sensors in computers, phones and vehicles.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: it is the main alloying element in cast aluminum (engine blocks, wheels) and, as ferrosilicon, is used to deoxidize steel.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: it is the raw material of silicones, used in sealants, lubricants, medical implants and technical materials for construction and industry.

Tantalum (Ta)

Extraction

Tantalum comes from columbite-tantalite (coltan), which crystallizes in granitic pegmatites rich in rare elements and also accumulates in alluvial deposits formed by their erosion; another source is tin smelting slag. The concentrate is dissolved with acids, purified by solvent extraction and reduced with sodium to obtain tantalum metal powder.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

DR Congo, Rwanda, Brazil, Nigeria and Australia.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: tantalum-bearing superalloys withstand extreme temperatures and corrosion in turbines, engines and aerospace components.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: tantalum capacitors, with high capacitance and small size, are used in mobile phones, computers, cars and communications equipment.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: its high biocompatibility and chemical resistance make it suitable for implants, surgical instruments and dental applications.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: tantalum carbide gives hardness and wear resistance to cutting and machining tools.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: used in corrosion-resistant equipment, such as heat exchangers and reactors operating under extreme conditions.

Titanium metal

Extraction

Titanium comes from ilmenite and rutile, which are obtained from coastal sand placers and from magmatic ilmenite deposits in mafic rocks, such as those in Norway and Canada. To obtain the metal, the ore is converted into titanium tetrachloride, which is reduced with magnesium (Kroll process) to produce titanium sponge; this is melted in vacuum furnaces to make ingots and alloys.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Australia, South Africa, Canada, China and Mozambique.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: its light, very strong alloys are used in armor, submarine hulls and fighter aircraft structures.
  • Aerospace: lightweight, high-temperature-resistant alloys used in fuselages, turbine blades and structural components of aircraft and jet engines.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: it withstands seawater and geothermal fluids, so it is used in the condensers of coastal power plants, in geothermal plants and in the blades of large steam turbines.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: thanks to its biocompatibility and corrosion resistance it is used in implants, prostheses, surgical instruments and dental applications.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: it withstands corrosive environments in desalination plants, marine installations, heat exchangers and energy systems.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: ilmenite and rutile are mainly used to make titanium dioxide, the white pigment in paints, plastics, paper and sunscreens.

Vanadium (V)

Extraction

Vanadium comes mainly from titaniferous magnetite, which is concentrated in layers within mafic igneous rocks. It is obtained as a co-product of iron: when steel is made from this ore, the vanadium remains in the slag, from which it is recovered. It is also extracted from petroleum residues and spent catalysts. The material is roasted and leached to obtain vanadium pentoxide, which is reduced to ferrovanadium.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, Russia, South Africa, Brazil and Australia.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: is part of titanium alloys used in structures, engines and aerospace components subjected to high stresses.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: vanadium redox flow batteries allow electricity to be stored on a large scale and make it easier to integrate renewable energy into the power grid.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: added as an alloying element to steels and tools to increase their strength, hardness, toughness and wear behavior.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: vanadium pentoxide acts as a catalyst in industrial processes, such as the production of sulfuric acid.
  • Construction and infrastructure: alloyed into high-strength structural steels used in reinforcement, beams and bridges.

Tungsten (W)

Extraction

Tungsten comes from wolframite and scheelite, which form in quartz veins and in skarns (limestones transformed next to granitic intrusions). It is mined underground and open-pit, and concentrated by gravity separation, taking advantage of its high density, and by flotation. The concentrate is chemically converted into ammonium paratungstate and reduced with hydrogen to metal powder, the basis of hard carbides.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, Vietnam, Russia, Bolivia and Rwanda.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: its high density and melting point make it useful in armor-piercing projectiles, armor and high-performance aerospace components.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: used in filaments, electrodes and electrical contacts, as well as in electronic components and specialized lighting equipment.
  • Nuclear energy: used as shielding in medical and industrial equipment and in fusion reactor components.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: gives high-temperature strength to steels and superalloys, and tungsten carbide is the basis of cutting and drilling tools.

Special clays

Extraction

Special clays have various origins: fibrous clays (sepiolite and palygorskite) and many bentonites (clay rocks made up mainly of smectites) form in lake basins and through the alteration of volcanic ash, as in the Madrid basin; kaolin and vermiculite, through the alteration of granites and micas; and talc and pyrophyllite, through metamorphism and hydrothermal alteration. They are worked in open-pit quarries, and crushed, dried, ground and classified; some are then activated with acid or chemically modified.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

United States, Spain, China, Turkey, South Africa and New Zealand.

Spain accounts for most of the world's sepiolite, the United States for most palygorskite, New Zealand for most halloysite, and South Africa leads in vermiculite. China is the world's leading producer of talc, followed by India, Brazil and the United States; pyrophyllite is mined mainly in South Korea, China and Brazil.

Strategic applications

  • Medicine and pharmacy: several clays are active ingredients in antidiarrheals and excipients in tablets, syrups and creams; talc is also used in cosmetics, and clay muds in mud therapy.
  • Nuclear energy: bentonite (a clay rock made up mainly of smectites such as montmorillonite) is used as a sealing barrier in landfills and waste repositories, including radioactive waste, thanks to its low permeability and swelling capacity.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: bentonite is used in drilling muds, as a binder for foundry sands and in iron ore pelletizing.
  • Construction and infrastructure: exfoliated vermiculite is added to lightweight concretes, plasters and thermal and fire-protection insulation.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: absorb oils and liquids, act as carriers for plant protection products and fertilizers, and are the basis of pet litter; vermiculite is used in growing media.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: kaolin and talc are fillers and coatings for paper, paints, plastics and rubber, and sepiolite and bentonite act as thickeners.
  • Glass and ceramics: kaolin, halloysite, talc and pyrophyllite are raw materials for porcelain, fine and technical ceramics, and refractories.

Aluminosilicates (andalusite, kyanite, sillimanite)

Extraction

Andalusite, kyanite and sillimanite are three minerals with the same composition (Al₂SiO₅) that form in aluminum-rich metamorphic rocks such as schists and gneisses; which one appears depends on pressure and temperature. They are mined in open pits and concentrated by gravity separation, magnetic separation or flotation. For refractory use they are calcined at over 1,300 °C and transformed into mullite.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

South Africa, United States, India, Peru, France and China.

South Africa leads the production of andalusite, the United States that of kyanite, and India that of sillimanite.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: used in ceramic shells to cast high-precision parts, such as turbine blades for aircraft engines.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: the mullite they form when calcined yields refractory bricks and castables for steel furnaces and ladles, and for glass, cement and aluminum furnaces.
  • Glass and ceramics: provide thermal shock resistance and low expansion to ceramic pieces and to kiln supports and plates.

Lead (Pb)

Extraction

Lead comes from galena, which forms in hydrothermal veins and in deposits within limestones and other sedimentary rocks, almost always together with zinc and silver. It is mined underground and open-pit, concentrated by flotation and smelted to obtain lead metal, which is refined while recovering the silver. More than half of the lead consumed today comes from recycling batteries.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · Australia · Peru · Mexico · Russia · United States · India · Bolivia.

China accounts, by a wide margin, for most of the world's lead mine production.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: manufacture of ammunition, due to its high density.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: main use of lead, in lead-acid batteries for vehicles and energy backup; also in counterweights, ballast and keels.
  • Nuclear energy: shielding used in medical radiology, nuclear facilities and industry, thanks to its high density, very effective at attenuating gamma radiation and X-rays.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: alloys with tin and other metals for technical solders and special components.
  • Construction and infrastructure: lead sheets used in roofing, soundproofing and protection against moisture.
  • Glass and ceramics: lead oxides used in special glasses, crystal glassware and ceramic glazes, to which they add brilliance, density and radiation-shielding capacity.

Zinc (Zn)

Extraction

Zinc comes from sphalerite, which forms in the same deposits as galena, often together with lead, silver and copper. It is mined underground and in open pits: in Spain, Reocín (Cantabria) was the leading mine, and today it is mined in the Iberian Pyrite Belt in Huelva. The ore is crushed and concentrated by flotation. The concentrate is roasted to turn it into oxide, which is dissolved in acid and electrolyzed to obtain high-purity zinc metal.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · Peru · Australia · India · United States · Mexico · Bolivia · Kazakhstan.

China accounts for most of the world's zinc mine production.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: forms the electrodes of alkaline batteries and zinc-air batteries.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: zinc oxide is used in ointments, barrier creams and sunscreens, and zinc in dietary supplements.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: it is alloyed with copper to make brass and is used in die-casting alloys for automotive parts and household appliances.
  • Construction and infrastructure: sheets, gutters and architectural elements of rolled zinc, valued for their durability and the protective patina they develop over time.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: essential micronutrient found in fertilizers, supplements and animal feed additives.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: protection of steel against corrosion with zinc coatings; this is its main use worldwide.

Molybdenum (Mo)

Extraction

Molybdenum comes from molybdenite, which occurs in porphyries: large masses of rock with disseminated sulfides, related to granitic intrusions. Much of it is obtained as a by-product of copper porphyries and the rest from dedicated mines. Molybdenite is separated by flotation, roasted to obtain molybdenum oxide, and this is converted into ferromolybdenum, chemical compounds or metal.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · Chile · United States · Peru · Mexico · Russia.

China and Chile account for much of world production; Chile obtains most of its molybdenum as a by-product of copper mining.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: components of turbines, aerospace engines and equipment subjected to extreme temperature conditions.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: electronic components, displays and special filaments.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: alloying element in stainless steels and high-strength steels, giving them hardness and resistance to corrosion and high temperatures.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: oil refining processes, such as hydrodesulfurization, and chemical production.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: molybdenum disulfide is used as a high-performance solid lubricant, and molybdates in pigments and industrial additives.

Iron (Fe)

Extraction

Iron comes mainly from banded iron formations, layers of oxides that precipitated in the seas more than 1,800 million years ago and are mined in huge open-pit mines in Australia and Brazil. Other deposits, such as those of Biscay or Alquife (Granada), were formed by hydrothermal fluids that replaced limestones and dolostones. The ore is crushed, concentrated and agglomerated, and in the blast furnace it is reduced with coke to obtain pig iron, which is refined to produce steel. Much steel is also made from scrap.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Australia · Brazil · China · India · Russia · South Africa · Ukraine · Canada.

Australia and Brazil account for most of the world's iron ore exports.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: basis of the steel used in armor, helmets, warships, military vehicles and most conventional weaponry.
  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: steel car bodies, engines and mechanical parts, and the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) in many electric-car batteries.
  • Energy transition / renewable energy: wind towers, oil pipelines, gas pipelines and power plant structures.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: basis of stainless steels, carbon steels and high-performance ferrous alloys.
  • Construction and infrastructure: steel is the basis of the beams, reinforcement and frameworks that support most modern buildings and infrastructure.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: iron oxides are the red, yellow and black pigments in paints, concrete and ceramics.

Silver (Ag)

Extraction

Silver occurs in hydrothermal veins, sometimes in its own deposits, such as those of Mexico and Peru, but mostly it accompanies lead, zinc, copper and gold ores; that is why most of it is obtained as a by-product. The ore is concentrated by flotation or dissolved by cyanidation, and the metal is separated at the smelter and refined by electrolysis.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Mexico · Peru · China · Russia · Poland · Chile · Australia · Bolivia.

For centuries, Mexico has been the world's largest silver producer.

Strategic applications

  • Energy transition / renewable energy: silver conductive pastes used in the manufacture of photovoltaic cells.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: it is the best conductor of electricity and heat among metals: it is used in contacts, circuits and electronic components, and its compounds in photography.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: antimicrobial properties used in dressings, catheters and medical coatings.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: catalyst in the production of ethylene oxide and formaldehyde.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: component of mirrors and reflective coatings.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: manufacture of jewelry, silverware and bullion coins, prized for its luster and its value as a safe haven against economic uncertainty.

Sulfur (S)

Extraction

Today almost all sulfur is obtained as a by-product of purifying oil and natural gas, which contain hydrogen sulfide: this is converted into elemental sulfur by the Claus process. Another part is recovered by roasting metal sulfides. Mining of native sulfur deposits, in evaporites and volcanic areas, is now very minor.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · United States · Russia · Saudi Arabia · United Arab Emirates · Canada · Kazakhstan · Iran.

Most of the world's sulfur comes from the oil and gas industry, not from mining.

Strategic applications

  • Energy storage, electric vehicles and mobility: sulfuric acid is the electrolyte of lead-acid batteries, and sulfur is being researched for lithium-sulfur batteries.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: sulfuric acid is used in the leaching of copper, nickel, cobalt, uranium and other metals.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: rubber vulcanization and the manufacture of pigments, detergents, paper and pharmaceuticals.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: its main use is sulfuric acid, used to make phosphate fertilizers; it also corrects sulfur-poor soils and forms fungicides.
  • Civil security and risk protection: traditional component of black powder and pyrotechnic mixtures.

Chromium (Cr)

Extraction

Chromium comes almost entirely from chromite, which separates from mafic and ultramafic magmas and accumulates in layers, as in the Bushveld Complex (South Africa), or in pods within peridotites. It is mined underground and open-pit, concentrated by gravity separation and smelted in electric furnaces with coal to produce ferrochrome, used mainly for stainless steel.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

South Africa · Kazakhstan · Turkey · India · Finland · Zimbabwe.

South Africa and Kazakhstan account for most of world production; Finland is the leading producer in the European Union.

Strategic applications

  • Defense and security: special steels and alloys for armor and military equipment, providing resistance to corrosion and wear under extreme conditions.
  • Aerospace: components that withstand high temperatures in turbines, engines and aerospace equipment.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: main use of chromium, which from 10.5% makes steel stainless; chromite is also used in refractories and foundry sands.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: decorative and technical chrome plating to protect against corrosion and wear, and chromium salts used in pigments, leather tanning and wood preservation.

Mercury (Hg)

Extraction

Mercury comes from cinnabar, which forms in low-temperature hydrothermal veins; Almadén (Ciudad Real) was for centuries the largest deposit in the world. The ore was heated in furnaces: the mercury was released as vapor and condensed as liquid metal. Today primary mining is banned in the European Union and mercury is recovered as a by-product of other metallurgical processes and from recycling.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · Tajikistan · Kyrgyzstan · Mexico · Peru.

Historically, Almadén (Spain) was the largest mercury mine in the world and ceased mining in 2003; today it is a World Heritage Site together with Idrija (Slovenia).

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: fluorescent and mercury-vapor lamps, being progressively replaced by LED technology.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: dental amalgams, which the European Union is gradually phasing out.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: gold amalgamation in artisanal mining, a highly polluting use that international regulations aim to eradicate.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: mercury cells for the production of chlorine and caustic soda, being phased out, and some catalysts.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: vermilion pigment, obtained from cinnabar, historically used in painting and decoration for its intense red color.
  • Advanced instrumentation: thermometers, barometers and pressure gauges, whose manufacture is banned or restricted in the EU.

Gold (Au)

Extraction

Gold is deposited in quartz veins and in large disseminated deposits from hydrothermal fluids, and erosion of those rocks accumulates it in alluvial placers. In placers it is separated by gravity; in hard rock, the ore is ground, the gold is dissolved with cyanide and recovered with activated carbon. It is then smelted and refined. It is also obtained as a by-product of copper and from recycling jewelry and electronics.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · Russia · Australia · Canada · United States · Ghana · Peru · Indonesia.

Production is widely spread across many countries; China is the leading producer, with around one tenth of the world total.

Strategic applications

  • Aerospace: reflective and protective coatings against radiation and heat, and high-reliability contacts.
  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: contacts, connectors and microcircuits that require reliable, oxidation-free conduction.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: dentistry, implantable devices and nanoparticles for diagnosis and therapies.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: catalysts in chemical processes and selective oxidation reactions.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: main use of gold; as bars, coins and central bank reserves it is also a safe-haven asset against economic uncertainty.

Zeolites

Extraction

Industrial zeolites come from volcanic ash altered in alkaline lakes and shallow seabeds. They are mined in open pits, and the ore is crushed, ground and screened. Collector specimens, by contrast, crystallize in cavities in basalts and are extracted by hand. Synthetic zeolites are also made for catalysts and molecular sieves.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · United States · South Korea · Japan · Slovakia · Cuba · Jordan · Turkey.

China accounts for most of the world's production of natural zeolites; the United States and South Korea also stand out in the manufacture of high-value synthetic zeolites.

Strategic applications

  • Nuclear energy: selective capture of radioactive cesium and strontium in contaminated water, a key role in decontamination after nuclear accidents such as Fukushima.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: catalysts in the catalytic cracking of petroleum and in petrochemical processes, and molecular sieves that separate and dry gases and liquids according to the size of their molecules.
  • Construction and infrastructure: pozzolanic additions in cements.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: soil improver that retains water and nutrients, and additive in animal feed.
  • Environmental management and water treatment: ion exchange to remove ammonium, heavy metals and other contaminants, and water softening in detergents, where they replace phosphates.

Tourmalines

Extraction

Tourmalines are borosilicates that crystallize mainly in granitic pegmatites, in the last stages of magma crystallization, when boron becomes concentrated. They are extracted in small mines, often artisanal, by carefully opening the pegmatite pockets so as not to damage the crystals. Gem-quality specimens are cut; the rest is ground for industrial uses.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Brazil · Nigeria · Mozambique · Madagascar · Afghanistan · Namibia · United States.

Brazil has historically been the leading producer and exporter of gem-quality tourmalines, followed by African countries such as Nigeria, Mozambique and Madagascar, which have gained great importance in recent decades.

Strategic applications

  • Advanced instrumentation: it generates electricity when squeezed or heated, which has been used in pressure sensors.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: main use of the group, highly valued for its enormous variety of colors and color combinations.

Tin (Sn)

Extraction

Tin comes from cassiterite, which forms in veins and in granites altered by fluids (greisen), and which erosion later accumulates in alluvial and coastal placers. In placers it is extracted with dredges and concentrated by gravity, taking advantage of its high density; in hard rock, it is mined underground. The concentrate is smelted with coal and refined to obtain high-purity tin.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China · Indonesia · Myanmar (Burma) · Peru · Bolivia · Brazil · DR Congo · Nigeria.

China and Indonesia together account for more than half of the world's tin mine production.

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: main use of tin, in solder alloys (tin-silver-copper) for electronic circuits and surface-mount boards.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: bronze (with copper), pewter and other low-melting technical alloys.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: organotin compounds used as PVC stabilizers and biocides.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: protective coating of steel sheet for food packaging and tin cans.
  • Glass and ceramics: bath of molten tin on which high-quality flat glass is made, using the float process employed for virtually all flat glass today.
  • Advanced instrumentation: niobium-tin alloy used in superconducting magnets for magnetic resonance imaging and particle accelerators.

Garnets

Extraction

Garnets crystallize mainly in metamorphic rocks, such as schists, gneisses and amphibolites. Industrial garnet, used as an abrasive and for waterjet cutting, comes largely from beach and alluvial sands, where it is concentrated by its density and hardness, and is separated from other heavy minerals by gravity and magnetism. Gem-quality specimens are selected and cut separately.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

India · China · Australia · United States · South Africa · Turkey · Russia.

India and China dominate the production of industrial garnet for abrasives, while Tanzania, Kenya, Madagascar and Mozambique stand out for gem-quality garnets.

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: synthetic garnets (YAG, GGG) used in solid-state lasers and electronic substrates.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: waterjet cutting, abrasive blasting and the manufacture of garnet paper and sandpaper.
  • Environmental management and water treatment: filter medium in drinking water and wastewater treatment plants, thanks to its hardness and density.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: gem-quality varieties, highly prized for their wide range of colors.

Gemstones

Extraction

Gemstones are very different minerals (diamond, corundum, beryl, topaz, quartz…) that form in diverse settings: kimberlites and pegmatites, metamorphic rocks and cavities in volcanic rocks, such as amethyst geodes. Being hard and dense, they are concentrated by erosion in alluvial gravels, where much of the supply comes from. Diamond is mined in large mines; the others, often by artisanal mining. They are then sorted and cut.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Russia · Botswana · Canada · DR Congo · Australia (diamond); Myanmar and Sri Lanka (ruby and sapphire); Colombia and Zambia (emerald); Brazil and Madagascar (pegmatite gems).

Russia, Botswana, Canada and DR Congo account for most of the world's diamond production, while Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Colombia, Zambia, Brazil and Madagascar stand out for colored gems.

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: synthetic diamond is used in optical windows, heat sinks and high-power electronics; synthetic corundum in watchmaking and precision components.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: industrial diamond, natural and synthetic, is used in very hard cutting, polishing and drilling tools.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: main and most valuable use: diamond, ruby, sapphire and emerald are the most prized gems, and the finest pieces are also used as an investment.

Micas

Extraction

Micas crystallize in granitic pegmatites, granites and metamorphic rocks such as schists and gneisses. Sheet mica, the most valuable, is extracted by hand from pegmatites to preserve the large crystals, which are split into thin sheets. Flake mica, more abundant, is obtained as a by-product of feldspar and kaolin or from schists, and is ground into mica powder.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

India · China · Russia · Madagascar · Brazil · United States · South Korea.

India is the world's leading producer of high-quality sheet mica, while China leads the production of flake mica and mica powder.

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: historical and strategic use for its thermal stability and dielectric properties, in capacitors, insulators and electrical components.
  • Medicine and pharmacy: pearlescent pigments and pearl effect in makeup, creams and personal care products.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: filler in engineering plastics, improving their stability and insulation, and additive in drilling muds to seal porous formations.
  • Construction and infrastructure: component of joint compounds for plasterboard, mortars and roofing materials.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: functional filler that provides gloss, strength and dimensional stability.

Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)

Extraction

Calcium carbonate occurs in nature as calcite, the mineral of limestones and marbles, and as aragonite, which is scarcer and forms shells, corals and marine oolitic sands. Limestone is extracted in open-pit quarries, crushed, ground and classified, and part of it is calcined at about 900 °C to obtain lime; aragonite sands, such as those of the Bahamas, are extracted by dredging. Precipitated calcium carbonate, in the form of calcite or aragonite, is also manufactured for high-purity fillers.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

China, United States, India, Russia and Brazil.

China accounts, by a wide margin, for most of the world's production of limestone and lime.

The Bahamas are the main producer of aragonite sand.

Strategic applications

  • Medicine and pharmacy: source of calcium in antacids, supplements and food additives, and a common excipient in the manufacture of pharmaceutical tablets.
  • Metallurgical and steel industry: flux in blast furnaces, where it helps separate impurities from the iron ore in the form of slag.
  • Construction and infrastructure: aggregate in concrete and road surfaces, and main raw material for making cement.
  • Agriculture, food security and packaging: amendment for acidic soils and component of animal feed and fertilizers; crushed shells, made of aragonite, are used as a calcium supplement for poultry.
  • Environmental management and water treatment: adjusting the pH and alkalinity of water, and capturing sulfur in flue gas desulfurization.
  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: mineral filler, natural or precipitated, in the form of calcite or aragonite, that gives whiteness, opacity and strength to paper, paints and plastics.
  • Glass and ceramics: raw material for glass, to which it adds calcium, and for ceramic glazes and pastes.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: nacre and pearls are made of aragonite, and marbles such as that of Macael (Almería) are used as ornamental stone.

Lapis lazuli (ornamental rock rich in lazurite)

Extraction

Lapis lazuli is a metamorphic rock that forms when impure limestones are transformed by the heat and fluids of nearby granitic intrusions. It owes its blue color to lazurite, with golden specks of pyrite and white veins of calcite. The best deposits, in the Badakhshan mountains (Afghanistan), have been worked for about 6,000 years in underground mines, with blocks selected by hand.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Afghanistan accounts for practically all world production of gem quality, with the Sar-e-Sang mines, in Badakhshan province, worked almost continuously for more than 6,000 years.

To a lesser extent it is also mined in Chile, Russia, Pakistan, Italy, Mongolia, the United States and Canada.

Strategic applications

  • Paints, pigments, coatings and lubricants: ground and purified, it yields natural ultramarine, a high-quality blue pigment historically used in Renaissance and Baroque painting.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: used since Antiquity in Egypt and Mesopotamia; today it is worked into beads, cabochons, mosaics, inlays and carved decorative objects.

Olivine ((Mg,Fe)₂SiO₄)

Extraction

Olivine is one of the first minerals to crystallize in silica-poor magmas and, because of its density, it accumulates at the bottom of magma chambers, forming dunites, rocks made almost entirely of olivine, and peridotites, in which it is accompanied by pyroxenes. These rocks are worked in open-pit quarries, as in Norway, and crushed and ground to the size required for each industrial use.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Norway, United States, Spain, Austria and Turkey.

Norway is traditionally the world's largest producer and exporter of industrial olivine.

Strategic applications

  • Metallurgical and steel industry: flux in blast furnaces, molding sand and refractory, and blasting abrasive that does not generate quartz dust.
  • Environmental management and water treatment: its accelerated weathering is being tested to capture CO₂ from the atmosphere.
  • Jewelry, ornamentation and store of value: its transparent gem-quality variety is peridot, the birthstone for August.

Pollucite (Cs(AlSi₂O₆))

Extraction

Pollucite is the main ore of cesium. It forms in highly evolved granitic pegmatites, in their innermost zones, together with lithium, tantalum and beryllium minerals, as at the Tanco mine (Canada). It is extracted by selective underground mining, hand-sorted and concentrated, and the cesium is obtained by dissolving the mineral with acids.

Main minerals

Main producing countries

Canada accounts for virtually all of the world's production, with the Bernic Lake deposit (Manitoba), which holds more than two thirds of the world's known reserves.

There are also smaller deposits in Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Strategic applications

  • Electronics, semiconductors and digital technologies: photoelectric cells, vacuum tubes and scintillation counters.
  • Chemical industry and catalysis: main source of cesium, whose formate is a dense, low-toxicity fluid for drilling deep wells; also used in catalysis.
  • Advanced instrumentation: the isotope cesium-133 defines the international unit of time (the second) and is used in the most precise frequency standards.

Sodalite (Na₈(Al₆Si₆O₂₄)Cl₂)

Extraction
